doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

chapter: Becoming a jazz fan and musician
title: Self-taught guitar and the love of rhythm guitar
summary: Pelote taught himself guitar from Mel Bay books and admired rhythm players like Eddie Condon, Freddie Green and Dick McDonough.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: And so do you pursue this in higher education? How did this passion delve into a career?

Okay, when I went to college — oh I played guitar all throughout high school, pretty much on my own. I mean I am a self-taught guitar player. I didn’t take lessons. And I just listened a lot, I got the Mel Bay books for guitar and I went through the whole chord system so I could have a system. I didn’t want just a bunch of chords, I wanted a system so that I could play whatever was put in front of me by just using this system. So I did that. Of course I’ve since learned I was playing these crazy chords, didn’t have to play with any — that’s another story. And I fell in love with the whole concept of playing in a rhythm section and just playing chords. To me that was the greatest thing in the world, that somebody would devote themselves to just doing that. Eddie Condon was my hero. I loved Eddie Condon for just sitting there and doing that, and Freddie Green of course. But there were other rhythm guitars. Everybody talks about Freddie Green, but there’s other ways to play rhythm guitar. His is not the only way. Marty Grosz makes that quite clear today, that there are other types of rhythm guitar that you can play. I mean Dick McDonough was that wonderful rhythm guitarist, as were, I can just rattle off a bunch of names. Clayton “Sunshine” Duerr, who played with Louie Prima and, or Mezz Mezzrow. He played with Mezz Mezzrow and his orchestra. So there’s a whole bunch of guys like that that were just great rhythm guitar players, without necessarily sounding like Freddie Green. So that became my passion. And so I went to college to be basically, I went to be a writer originally but I went on the wrong day. So there was no orientation day, so there was nobody from the English department there, but there was a guy from the music department, so I went over to him. His name was Chester Fanning Smith. He was a classical pianist.
